Building Passport Seva Kendra on Salesforce: Project Log #1 — Vision, Architecture & Local Setup

This is the first entry in an ongoing build log for Passport Seva Kendra (PSK) — a from-scratch Salesforce implementation modelling the offices that process Indian passport applications. This is an independent portfolio project, not affiliated with any government body. Rather than publishing a new post for every commit, this log grows in place: new work gets folded into the post it belongs under, so the series stays a small number of long, complete references instead of a scattered stream. This post covers why the project exists, how it's architected at a high level, and how to pull it down and run it yourself.

Why this project exists

PSK is a demonstration of core Salesforce engineering on a genuinely tricky domain: a government-style service process with strict lifecycle rules, personal data handling, and eventual integrations (appointment scheduling, SMS/WhatsApp notifications, fraud signals). The goal isn't a toy CRUD app — it's a small, deliberately-scoped org that shows data modelling judgment, automation, security/sharing design, and (in later phases) third-party integration via n8n, Twilio, and AI.

The core design decision: few objects, many fields

The biggest architectural call made before any metadata was written: the entire passport application lifecycle — from a half-finished draft to a delivered booklet — lives on one object, Passport_Application__c, driven by a Status picklist and Record Types. It would have been easy to reach for a new object per stage (a "Draft Application" object, a "Submitted Application" object, a "Granted Passport" object). That's the wrong model here: a half-finished form is the same record in Draft status, not a different kind of thing. Modelling it as separate objects would mean migrating data across objects every time a citizen's application progresses — fragile, and it obscures the fact that it's fundamentally one entity with a lifecycle.

Everything else in the schema — appointments, payments, document checklists, police verification, objections, renewals, notifications, risk flags — hangs off that one root object as either a master-detail child (tightly owned, cascade-deleted with the parent) or a lookup (independently owned, survives the parent). Which one was used for which object is a deliberate call, covered in the data-model post in this series.

Compliance by design: the Aadhaar rule

One rule threads through the whole schema: the Aadhaar number itself is never stored. Only two fields exist for it — Aadhaar_Verified__c (a checkbox) and Aadhaar_Token__c (an opaque token, not the number). This follows India's DPDP Act principle of data minimisation: don't collect and retain sensitive personal data your process doesn't actually need to operate. In a production system, that token field would sit behind Salesforce Shield Platform Encryption; in this portfolio build it's a plain text field with the discipline of never populating it with anything sensitive.

Environment

  • Org: Salesforce Developer Edition, alias psk-dev
  • Tooling: Salesforce CLI (sf), SFDX source format
  • Source control: Git, hosted at github.com/imswarnil/Passport-Seva-Kendra-Salesforce
  • Deploy workflow: incremental — object shell, then fields, then relationships, then record types, then FLS, then layouts, then validation rules — confirming each step against the org before moving to the next

A security lesson, early

Worth logging honestly: an early retrieve from the org pulled down an inherited Apex class (OpenAIChatController, left over from a CRM Analytics/Wave demo template) that contained a hardcoded OpenAI API key in plain text. Before the repository was ever pushed publicly, that class was deleted from both the org and the codebase, all 42 profile references to it were cleaned up, and — since the key had landed in the very first local commit — the entire git history was rebuilt from a clean single root commit rather than trying to scrub one commit out of a chain. The key itself was still rotated regardless, on the assumption that anything that touched disk in plaintext should be treated as compromised. Lesson: audit anything a template or scaffold brings in before it goes anywhere near a remote.

Running this project locally

The whole project is an SFDX source-format repository. To pull it down and start working against your own Salesforce org:

1. Prerequisites

sf version                 # confirm the Salesforce CLI is installed
git --version

If you don't have the CLI: npm install --global @salesforce/cli

2. Clone the repo

git clone https://github.com/imswarnil/Passport-Seva-Kendra-Salesforce.git
cd Passport-Seva-Kendra-Salesforce

3. Authenticate to a Salesforce org

You'll need your own Developer Edition (or scratch/sandbox) org — this project doesn't ship with access to the original one.

sf org login web --alias psk-dev --instance-url https://login.salesforce.com
sf config set target-org=psk-dev

4. Deploy the metadata

# deploy everything
sf project deploy start --source-dir force-app

# or deploy one object/component at a time while reviewing
sf project deploy start --source-dir force-app/main/default/objects/Passport_Application__c

5. Assign yourself the app's permission set

sf org assign permset --name PSK_App_Access

Custom fields are invisible until FLS is granted — this permission set is what makes every PSK field readable/editable for the assigned user.

6. Run the Apex tests

sf apex run test --test-level RunLocalTests --code-coverage --result-format human

7. Re-sync from the org after making changes in Setup

sf project retrieve start --manifest manifest/package.xml

What's next

This post will keep growing as the environment and workflow evolve — new sections get added here rather than spun into new posts. The next post in the series covers the full data model: all eleven objects, how they relate, and why. After that: the branding and publishing setup for this very blog.

The Data Model: Every Object in Passport Seva Kendra, Explained

Part of the ongoing Passport Seva Kendra build log. This post is the living reference for the full data model — as new objects, fields, or relationships get added to the org, they get folded into this post rather than spawning a new one. Read the first post in this series for the project's vision and how to run it locally.

The roadmap

#ObjectAPI NameRelationship to ApplicationPurpose
1Passport ApplicationPassport_Application__c— (root)Full lifecycle, draft to delivered
2PSK OfficePSK__cLookup from ApplicationA physical service centre
3Appointment SlotSlot__cMaster-Detail to PSK OfficeA bookable capacity block at a centre
4AppointmentAppointment__cMaster-Detail (dual) to Application & SlotJunction: Application × Slot
5Document Checklist ItemDocument_Checklist_Item__cMaster-DetailRequired/received documents
6ObjectionObjection__cMaster-DetailAn issue raised on an application
7Police VerificationPolice_Verification__cLookupThe PV process
8PaymentPayment__cMaster-DetailA fee payment
9RenewalRenewal__cLookup (×2)Upcoming-expiry outreach
10Notification LogNotification_Log__cLookupEvery SMS/WhatsApp sent (Twilio idempotency)
11Risk FlagRisk_Flag__cLookupFraud/anomaly flags

Later phases (not yet built) add a Visa department, fulfilment tracking, and Custom Metadata Types for fee/SLA configuration.

Master-detail vs. lookup: the decision that mattered most

Six child objects had to be classified as either master-detail (owned and destroyed with the parent) or lookup (independent, survives the parent). The rule applied consistently: operational/process children are master-detail; audit and outreach children are lookups.

  • Master-detail — Slot→PSK Office, Appointment→Application+Slot, Document Checklist Item→Application, Objection→Application, Payment→Application. If the application is deleted, these have no reason to exist independently, and Salesforce cascades the delete automatically.
  • Lookup — Police Verification, Renewal, Notification Log, Risk Flag, all →Application. These are explicitly not cascade-deleted. A notification log is an audit trail — it should outlive the record it refers to, the same way you don't shred a mail receipt because the letter it proves was sent got thrown away. Police Verification was called out as a lookup in the original spec specifically to keep that verification history intact independent of the application record's lifecycle.

One subtlety with master-detail in Salesforce: a child object with a master-detail relationship cannot have its own independent sharing model — its sharingModel must be ControlledByParent. This tripped the first deploy attempt for three of the objects (Salesforce rejected Private outright), which is a useful thing to know before you design a junction object's sharing.

Object #1 — Passport Application, in full

Passport_Application__c is the heart of the system: 55 fields across eight logical groups.

  • Lifecycle — Status__c (Draft → Submitted → Payment Pending → Paid → Document Verification → Police Verification → Granting → Printing → Dispatch → Delivered, plus Rejected/Cancelled), Payment_Status__c, stage timestamps, and lookups to Applicant (Account) and PSK Office.
  • Applicant Details — name, DOB, gender, family names, marital status, contact info.
  • Address — full Indian address including a 35-value State picklist.
  • Application Details — Passport Category (Ordinary/Diplomatic/Official) which controls a dependent picklist, Clearance Level (only Diplomatic/Official categories show Ambassador/Consular/Minister or Govt Deputation/Delegation); booklet pages, validity years, Tatkal flag, minor/guardian handling, re-issue fields.
  • Payment — fee, reference, date, mode.
  • Verification & Compliance — the Aadhaar-token pair described above, document/PV status, a 0–100 risk score.
  • Consent & Notifications — a consent checkbox that gates all future Twilio sends, plus a timestamp for DPDP audit purposes.
  • Derived (formula) — Applicant_Age__c, Is_Minor__c, Is_Draft__c, all computed rather than stored.

Six Record Types represent the real-world passport types: Fresh, Re-issue, Tatkal, Lost/Damaged, Minor, Diplomatic/Official — each surfacing a different subset of fields via Dynamic Forms rather than duplicating the object.

Four validation rules enforce data quality only at the point it matters: a Draft can be saved with almost nothing filled in, but the moment Status__c moves past Draft, core identity fields become mandatory, a minor's guardian consent is required, granting is blocked while payment is outstanding, and a delivered application can't be walked backward to an earlier stage. This "enforce on submit, not on save" pattern is what makes a multi-step public-facing form usable — citizens can leave a half-finished application and come back to it.

Field-level security and the permission set

Every custom field is invisible by default the moment it's deployed via metadata — this catches people out constantly. A single permission set, PSK_App_Access, grants object CRUD and field-level read/edit across all eleven objects, with two carve-outs: formula fields are read-only, and master-detail relationship fields are excluded from field permissions entirely (Salesforce doesn't allow FLS on a required master-detail field — it's always visible by definition). The System Administrator profile doesn't need explicit object permissions here, since it already carries Modify All Data / View All Data, which bypasses object-level CRUD org-wide; FLS is the layer the permission set actually needed to provide.

A small but satisfying roll-up

Slot__c carries a roll-up summary field, Booked_Count__c, counting its child Appointments, plus a formula field Is_Available__c (Booked_Count__c < Capacity__c). It's a small piece of declarative automation, but it's the first bit of the scheduling logic that later appointment-booking flows will depend on.

Smoke-testing the whole graph

Before committing, every relationship type got exercised together in one anonymous Apex script: create a PSK Office, a Slot, book an Appointment (confirm the roll-up ticks up), attach a Document Checklist Item, Objection, and Payment (all master-detail), attach a Police Verification, Renewal, Notification Log, and Risk Flag (all lookups) — then delete the parent Application and verify the master-detail children vanish with it while the lookup children survive, orphaned with a null parent reference, exactly as designed. The roll-up correctly recalculated back down after the cascade-delete too.

Field history tracking

Five fields are tracked for history: Status__c, Payment_Status__c, Passport_Category__c, Aadhaar_Verified__c, Documents_Verified__c — the fields where "who changed this, and when" genuinely matters for an audit trail on a government-style process.

Conventions used throughout

  • Objects: singular label, PascalCase API name with underscores (Passport_Application__c)
  • Fields: descriptive, no abbreviations (Police_Verification_Type__c, never PV_Typ__c)
  • Picklists: restricted value sets throughout
  • Record types: plain business names, no prefixing
  • Sharing: Private on anything holding personal data; Public Read Only on pure reference data (PSK Office, Slot)

Next in this series: the branding and publishing setup behind this blog itself.

Theme, Branding & Publishing This Build Log

Part of the ongoing Passport Seva Kendra build log — this post covers the "meta" layer: why this is being documented in public at all, and how the blog itself was set up. Like the rest of this series, it'll keep growing in place rather than splitting into new posts.

Why document this in public

A private repo proves you can write code. A documented build proves you can think — that the object model, the security fix, the master-detail-vs-lookup calls all had reasoning behind them, not just outcomes. That's the point of this log: it should be genuinely useful to someone building their own Salesforce portfolio project, not just a changelog.

Platform choice

This build log runs on Ghost, organized under a #project internal tag so it can sit alongside other, unrelated writing on the same site without polluting the main feed's navigation. Posts in this series use a small, deliberately public set of tags — Salesforce, Data Modeling, Portfolio, GovTech — so they're discoverable on their own even outside the #project grouping.

Brand assets

Logo and favicon assets for the project have been uploaded through Ghost's own asset manager (Settings → Design). [[Note the specific asset filenames/dimensions here once finalized — e.g. logo.svg, favicon.png, social share image]]

Color palette

The palette follows the tone of the subject matter: calm, official, legible — closer to a government portal's restraint than a typical SaaS product's brightness. [[Insert the actual palette here once locked in — primary/accent/background hex values, and the reasoning if any (e.g. matching Indian passport office signage, accessibility contrast ratios chosen)]]

Custom domain

The site is published on a custom domain rather than the default Ghost(Pro) subdomain. [[Insert the actual domain here, plus anything notable about the DNS/CNAME setup, once finalized]]

How this series stays maintainable

Rather than one post per commit — which would bury the small number of decisions that actually matter under a wall of "added field X" entries — this build log deliberately stays at three long-form posts:

  1. Vision, Architecture & Local Setup — the why, and how to run the project yourself
  2. The Data Model — every object, every relationship, every design call
  3. Theme, Branding & Publishing — this post

As the project grows — automation (Flow/Apex triggers), the n8n/Twilio integration, the Visa department phase — new material gets folded into whichever of these it belongs under, and a genuinely new phase of work gets its own post only when it doesn't fit any umbrella already established. That keeps the series skimmable at three entries deep, rather than thirty.

Follow the build

The full source is public: github.com/imswarnil/Passport-Seva-Kendra-Salesforce.

How this series stays maintainable

Rather than one post per commit — which would bury the small number of decisions that actually matter under a wall of "added field X" entries — this build log deliberately stays at three long-form posts:

  1. Vision, Architecture & Local Setup — the why, and how to run the project yourself
  2. The Data Model — every object, every relationship, every design call
  3. Theme, Branding & Publishing — this post

As the project grows — automation (Flow/Apex triggers), the n8n/Twilio integration, the Visa department phase — new material gets folded into whichever of these it belongs under, and a genuinely new phase of work gets its own post only when it doesn't fit any umbrella already established. That keeps the series skimmable at three entries deep, rather than thirty.
